cosy-lesson.title: Session 3: Changing Our Brains & Reclaiming Solitude

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: to introduce the topic and clarify key target vocabulary for the session.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Review the key vocabulary for this session below:

cosy-blockquote.p: Neuroplasticity – the physiological ability of the brain to reorganize itself by forming new neural pathways and structural connections throughout life.

p.em: Example: Our brain relies on neuroplasticity to adapt to our daily habits, meaning constant distraction physically reshapes our mind.

cosy-blockquote.p: To degrade ≠ improve – to lower the quality, strength, or physical condition of something over time ≠ to make it better or elevate its value.

p.em: Example: Continuous digital alerts degrade our working memory, whereas active reading exercises improve our baseline concentration.

cosy-blockquote.p: Mindfulness – the psychological state of being fully conscious, aware, and present in the current moment without judgment.

p.em: Example: Practicing daily mindfulness enables us to recognize digital cravings without immediately satisfying them.

cosy-blockquote.p: Focus – the center of activity, attraction, or attention, or the capacity to maintain concentration on a single task.

p.em: Example: Our deep focus is shattered whenever we pause to check an incoming text message.

cosy-blockquote.p: Memory – the faculty by which the mind stores, retains, and remembers past information and experiences.

p.em: Example: Our working memory is severely limited, which is why we forget what we are doing after looking at our lock screen.

cosy-blockquote.p: Reversible ≠ permanent – capable of being undone, altered, or returned to a previous state ≠ lasting or remaining unchanged forever.

p.em: Example: Fortunately, tech-induced brain damage is reversible if we change our environment, whereas some neurological changes are permanent.

cosy-blockquote.p: To sustain – to support, hold up, or maintain something physically or mentally for an extended period.

p.em: Example: Without an alarm, it is highly challenging to sustain undivided attention on a difficult book.

cosy-blockquote.p: Interruption – the sudden act of breaking the continuity or progress of a process, task, or conversation.

p.em: Example: Every minor digital interruption costs us several minutes as our brain struggles to refocus.

cosy-blockquote.p: Overwhelmed – feeling completely defeated, crushed, or physically and emotionally exhausted by an excessive amount of input or stress.

p.em: Example: We often feel completely overwhelmed when we try to manage multiple work chats simultaneously.

cosy-blockquote.p: Solitude – the state or situation of being entirely alone, often leading to a peaceful space for quiet reflection.

p.em: Example: Smartphones have destroyed our capacity for quiet solitude, as we are constantly surrounded by virtual voices.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: pair/group discussion on core session themes.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs or small breakout groups, discuss the following questions:

ol.li:
How does the mechanism of neuroplasticity explain our brain's physical adaptation to digital habits?
★ Do you find yourself losing patience with slow physical activities like cooking?

Why do digital alerts gradually degrade our capacity for undivided, sustained focus?
★ How many browser tabs do you typically have open while working on a single report?

How does practicing mindfulness help us intercept compulsive neural loops before they become habits?
★ Have you ever tried breathing slowly for two minutes when you felt a sudden craving to check your phone?

Why is our short-term working memory so vulnerable to a single, minor digital interruption?
★ Do you easily forget why you picked up your phone after seeing an unrelated alert?

Is the damage caused by screen reliance truly reversible, or do some structural changes remain permanent?
★ Have you noticed your concentration improving after taking a weekend break from screens?

Why is it so challenging to sustain a conversation when a participant's phone is visible on the table?
★ Does it annoy you when your partner looks at their screen while you are talking?

What does it mean to feel cognitively overwhelmed, and how does tech design accelerate this state?
★ Do you feel a physical sense of exhaustion after spending three hours on social feeds?

How has our constant virtual connection destroyed our capacity to appreciate peaceful solitude?
★ Do you enjoy being alone with your thoughts, or do you always play music or podcasts in the background?

Can we genuinely experience creative breakthroughs without experiencing periods of absolute boredom?
★ What is your best creative idea, and where were you physically when you thought of it?

How does the permanent availability of answers online weaken our natural biological curiosity?
★ Do you immediately look up trivial facts on the internet, or do you prefer to wonder about them?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: collaborative task or visual analysis in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, work together on the following task:

cosy-blockquote.p: - 🌳Analog SolitudeWalking in a forest for forty minutes without headphones or device tracking. 🎧Digital CompanionshipListening to an engaging podcast while tracking your steps and route on a map.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: 1-on-1 guided visual description and task response with teacher.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: deeper debate and statement evaluation in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, debate and state whether you agree or disagree with these statements:

ol.li:
Future neuro-devices will allow us to restore our working memory instantly using synthetic micro-currents. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Would you trust a medical device to repair your attention span?

Smartphones will eventually completely destroy our capacity to sustain long-term personal relationships. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Do you believe technology is already making couples feel more isolated from each other?

Future education will be entirely virtual, leaving children without any physical spaces for collective learning. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Would you allow your children to attend an online-only high school?

The human brain of the future will have a significantly degraded capacity for deep, analog solitude. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Do you think the desire to be alone is a natural biological trait or a cultural habit?

Brain scanners will eventually prove that screen use causes permanent cognitive damage in adults. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ If scientists proved that screens reduce IQ, would you change your habits?

In the future, corporate workers will take mandatory mindfulness breaks to restore their baseline focus. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Would you participate in an office meditation session if your boss requested it?

AI filters will soon shield our awareness from every single digital interruption, leaving only pure focus. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Would you let an AI filter decide which family messages are important enough to alert you?

Future societies will value analog, paper-based memories more than perfect digital photo archives. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Do you physically print your favorite vacation photos, or do they sit in the cloud?

The constant flux of global data will leave future generations feeling permanently overwhelmed. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Do you think modern news feeds are more stressful than useful?

Neuroplasticity will eventually allow the human brain to ignore all digital ads completely. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Do you already have a habit of ignoring side banner ads on web pages?

ul.li: Incorrect: This continuous alerts degrades my working memory. → Correct: These continuous alerts degrade my working memory. ((Grammatical alignment: 'alerts' is plural, requiring 'these' and the plural verb form 'degrade'))

Incorrect: We could sustained our focus yesterday. → Correct: We could sustain our focus yesterday. ((Modal verb grammar: modal verbs like 'could' must be followed by the base infinitive verb, not the past participle))

Incorrect: I felt completely overwhelming by the messages. → Correct: I felt completely overwhelmed by the messages. ((Underlined adjective choice. Use the '-ed' participle 'overwhelmed' to describe a passive feeling, and '-ing' to describe the active cause))
